sectionTitle: Chemistry — Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources

specStatements.text: The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

The gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned may include carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may also be released that form particulates in the atmosphere.
describe how carbon monoxide, soot (carbon particles), sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are produced by burning fuels
predict the products of combustion of a fuel given appropriate information about the composition of the fuel and the conditions in which it is used.
Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected.
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.
Particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.
describe and explain the problems caused by increased amounts of these pollutants in the air.

concepts.definition: The burning of a fuel in oxygen, releasing energy. The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
A substance released into the atmosphere that harms human health or the environment. Burning fuels is a major source of such substances.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur. The elements present in the fuel decide which pollutants its combustion can release.
Burning in a plentiful supply of air, so that the carbon in the fuel is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.
Burning in a limited supply of air, so that some carbon is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide or is released as solid carbon (soot), and some hydrocarbon may pass through unburned.
A gas, formula CO, produced when a carbon-containing fuel burns in a limited supply of air so that the carbon is not fully oxidised.
Solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in a limited supply of air. Soot and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.
Tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere, formed from solid particles such as soot and from unburned hydrocarbons released when fuels burn.
A gas, formula SO2, produced when sulfur present as an impurity in a fuel is oxidised as the fuel burns.
Gases formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the high temperatures reached inside an engine or a furnace. The nitrogen comes from the air, not from the fuel.
The gaseous water released when the hydrogen in a fuel is oxidised during burning. It is one of the gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned.
A gas that poisons the body. Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas, and because it is colourless and odourless it is not easily detected.
Rain made acidic by pollutants dissolving in it. Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain.
Damage to or irritation of the breathing system in humans. Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans.
The reduction in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface caused by particulates in the atmosphere. Particulates also cause health problems for humans.

misconceptions.question: Where does the nitrogen in the oxides of nitrogen from a car engine come from?
misconceptions.correct: From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine, which reacts with oxygen at the high temperature inside it.
misconceptions.misconception: When fuels burn, nitrogen from the air combines with other atoms, so nitrogen ends up in the products (such as nitrogen dioxide) whenever any fuel is burned.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from inside the fuel, and generalise that pattern to every pollutant.
misconceptions.correction: An engine draws in air as well as fuel, and air is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here whose key element does not come from the fuel.

misconceptions.question: Do all fuels contain sulfur?
misconceptions.correct: No. Most fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur, but sulfur is an impurity that is not always present.
misconceptions.misconception: Every fuel contains sulfur, so burning any fuel always releases sulfur dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfur dioxide appears in the specification's list of gases released when fuels burn, and students read a list of possible products as a list of guaranteed products.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says fuels 'may also contain some sulfur'. Sulfur dioxide is only released if the fuel actually contains sulfur, which is why low-sulfur fuels exist.

misconceptions.question: How would you know if carbon monoxide was leaking into a room?
misconceptions.correct: You would not notice it by sight or smell, because it is colourless and odourless, which is why detectors are used.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon monoxide has a strong smell, like the smell of car exhaust or of domestic gas, so people would notice it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of smelling exhaust fumes, and of the odour deliberately added to domestic gas, leads students to assume the dangerous gas is one they can smell.
misconceptions.correction: The smell of exhaust comes from other substances. Carbon monoxide itself is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous.

misconceptions.question: Which combustion products does the specification say cause acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the cause of acid rain, because it is the main gas released when fuels burn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant students hear about most, so it becomes the default answer for any harmful effect of burning fuels.
misconceptions.correction: In this specification carbon dioxide is linked to climate change, not to acid rain. Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

misconceptions.question: What effect on sunlight do particulates have?
misconceptions.correct: They cause global dimming, reducing the amount of sunlight that reaches the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Particulates add to global warming by trapping heat in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every pollutant gets filed under 'global warming', and the words 'global dimming' and 'global warming' look alike, so students blur the two.
misconceptions.correction: Particulates reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less light reaches the surface. That is global dimming. The specification also links particulates to health problems for humans.

misconceptions.question: When is carbon monoxide produced by a burning fuel?
misconceptions.correct: When the supply of air is limited, so combustion is incomplete and the carbon is not fully oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon monoxide is produced whenever a carbon-containing fuel burns, no matter how much air is available.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students memorise a list of combustion pollutants without attaching each one to the condition that produces it.
misconceptions.correction: With a plentiful supply of air the carbon is oxidised all the way to carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide appears only when the oxygen supply is limited.

misconceptions.question: Under what conditions is soot produced?
misconceptions.correct: When the supply of air is limited, so some carbon in the fuel is released as solid particles rather than being oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Soot is produced when there is plenty of oxygen, because a hotter, fiercer flame burns more of the fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate soot with a big, hot fire and do not connect the sooty yellow flame with a shortage of air.
misconceptions.correction: A plentiful air supply gives a clean flame and carbon dioxide. A limited air supply gives a sooty flame, because carbon is released as solid particles.

misconceptions.question: Are particulates gases?
misconceptions.correct: No. Particulates are tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Particulates are just another polluting gas, like carbon monoxide or sulfur dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particulates are mentioned alongside gases in the same part of the specification about what is released when fuels burn, so students treat them as one more item in a list of gases.
misconceptions.correction: The specification separates them: solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates. They are suspended solids, which is why they block sunlight and cause global dimming.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the hydrogen in a fuel when the fuel burns?
misconceptions.correct: It is oxidised to water, which is released as water vapour.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen is released as hydrogen gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of burning as breaking the fuel apart into its elements rather than as a reaction of the fuel with oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen. The hydrogen in the fuel combines with oxygen to make water, which appears in the exhaust gases as water vapour.

misconceptions.question: Is global dimming the same as damage to the ozone layer?
misconceptions.correct: No. Global dimming is less sunlight reaching the surface because particulates in the atmosphere block it.
misconceptions.misconception: Global dimming means the ozone layer has been destroyed, so light and radiation get through differently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hold a single 'damaged atmosphere' idea in which ozone holes, dimming and warming are all the same story.
misconceptions.correction: The specification links particulates to global dimming and to health problems in humans. Ozone depletion is a separate issue and is not what global dimming means.

misconceptions.question: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
misconceptions.correct: Because it is a toxic gas, and it is colourless and odourless so it is not easily detected.
misconceptions.misconception: It is dangerous because it is explosive and will catch fire if there is a spark.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate any gas leak in a house with a fire or explosion risk, which is the hazard they have been warned about most often.
misconceptions.correction: The hazard the specification gives is toxicity. Carbon monoxide poisons people, and because it cannot be seen or smelled they may not realise they are breathing it.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon monoxide cause acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: No. The specification gives sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen as the causes of acid rain.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon monoxide causes acid rain, because it is a harmful gas released by burning fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students group all combustion pollutants together and assume they share all the same harmful effects.
misconceptions.correction: Each pollutant has its own effects. Carbon monoxide is toxic; sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems and acid rain; particulates cause global dimming and health problems.

misconceptions.question: What is the black soot produced when a fuel burns?
misconceptions.correct: Soot is solid carbon: carbon from the fuel that has been released without being oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Soot is the sulfur or ash left behind when the fuel burns, not carbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a black solid residue to be leftover impurity, and they know fuels can contain sulfur, so they identify the sooty solid as sulfur or ash rather than as carbon from the fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Soot is unburned carbon. When the air supply is limited, some of the carbon in the fuel is released as fine solid particles instead of being oxidised to carbon dioxide. It is not the sulfur impurity, which leaves as sulfur dioxide gas.

mcqs.stem: A monitoring station in a city records carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates in the air above a busy road. What do these three pollutants have in common?

options.text: All three are released when fuels are burned
options.rationale: The specification names the combustion of fuels as a major source of atmospheric pollutants, and all three of these are released when fuels burn.

options.text: All three form from nitrogen in the air
options.rationale: Chosen by students who know air supplies the nitrogen for oxides of nitrogen and extend that origin to every pollutant in the list.

options.text: All three come from sulfur in the fuel
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe every fuel contains sulfur and that sulfur is behind all pollution from burning.

options.text: All three are gases like carbon monoxide
options.rationale: Students who think particulates are just another gas like CO wrongly class all three as gases.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what most fuels, including coal, contain?

options.text: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and always a little sulfur
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read sulfur dioxide in the list of combustion products as proof that sulfur is present in every fuel.

options.text: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and possibly some sulfur
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

options.text: Carbon and nitrogen, and possibly some sulfur
options.rationale: Selected by students who assume the nitrogen in oxides of nitrogen must have come from inside the fuel itself.

options.text: Sulfur and oxygen, and possibly some carbon
options.rationale: A student who knows fuels react with oxygen may wrongly place the oxygen inside the fuel rather than in the air around it.

mcqs.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in a plentiful supply of air. Which two substances are released?

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water vapour
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think carbon monoxide is formed whenever a fuel burns, rather than only when the air supply is limited.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Picked by students who expect sulfur dioxide from any fuel, even though a hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water vapour
options.rationale: With plenty of air the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: Selected by students who think burning splits the fuel into its elements, so the hydrogen comes off as hydrogen gas.

mcqs.stem: Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons are released from a burning fuel. What do they form in the atmosphere?

options.text: A gas called carbon monoxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat everything released from a burning fuel as a gas and reach for the most familiar one.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide in the air
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume any solid material left over must be the sulfur impurity in the fuel.

options.text: Carbon dioxide that causes acid rain
options.rationale: Students who think unburned hydrocarbons become CO2, and that CO2 causes acid rain, pick this.

options.text: Particulates in the air
options.rationale: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.

mcqs.stem: Petrol is burned inside a car engine and carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases. Why is carbon monoxide produced?

options.text: Nitrogen from the air combines with carbon atoms
options.rationale: Chosen by students who know the air takes part in engine reactions but attach the nitrogen to the carbon instead of the oxygen.

options.text: The oxygen supply is limited, so combustion is incomplete
options.rationale: Inside the engine the air supply is limited, so some carbon is only partly oxidised and carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide.

options.text: Sulfur in the petrol takes oxygen from the carbon
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe sulfur is present in all fuels and use it to explain any incomplete reaction.

options.text: The oxygen supply is plentiful, so carbon burns fully
options.rationale: Selected by students who reverse the condition and think a fierce, well supplied flame is the one that makes carbon monoxide and soot.

mcqs.stem: Oxides of nitrogen are found in the exhaust gases of a hot car engine. Where does the nitrogen in them come from?

options.text: From nitrogen compounds present inside the fuel
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume every element in an exhaust gas must have entered the engine as part of the fuel.

options.text: From sulfur impurities reacting with hot air
options.rationale: Picked by students who explain any unexpected exhaust gas by pointing to the sulfur impurity in the fuel.

options.text: From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine
options.rationale: Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and at the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen from the air.

options.text: From nitrogen given off as the fuel breaks up
options.rationale: Selected by students who picture combustion as splitting the fuel into elements rather than as a reaction with oxygen from the air.

mcqs.stem: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the hydrogen in the fuel is released as hydrogen gas rather than oxidised to water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide, water and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Picked by students who expect carbon monoxide from any burning fuel, ignoring the plentiful supply of air stated in the question.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, soot and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Selected by students who think soot is produced by a hot, well supplied flame rather than by a shortage of air.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: With plenty of air the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, the hydrogen to water, and the sulfur impurity to sulfur dioxide.

mcqs.stem: A gas heater burns methane in a room where the air vent has been blocked, so the oxygen supply is poor. Which product now appears that would not be formed with plenty of air?

options.text: Carbon monoxide
options.rationale: With a limited oxygen supply the carbon in the methane is only partly oxidised, so carbon monoxide is formed instead of carbon dioxide.

options.text: Nitrogen dioxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who link oxides of nitrogen to the fuel rather than to nitrogen and oxygen from the air at high temperature.

options.text: Unburned hydrogen
options.rationale: Picked by students who think a shortage of oxygen leaves the hydrogen in the methane to escape as hydrogen gas.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide gas
options.rationale: Selected by students who believe all fuels contain sulfur, even though methane contains only carbon and hydrogen.

mcqs.stem: Carbon monoxide leaks from a faulty boiler into a house. Why is this so dangerous?

options.text: It has a sharp smell that people learn to ignore
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the dangerous gas is one they can smell, as with the odour added to domestic gas.

options.text: It turns the water vapour in the room into acid
options.rationale: Picked by students who give carbon monoxide the acid rain effect that belongs to sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

options.text: It is toxic, and colourless and odourless so hard to spot
options.rationale: The specification states that carbon monoxide is a toxic gas and that it is colourless and odourless, so it is not easily detected.

options.text: It is explosive and can set the whole room alight
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat any gas leak in a house as a fire hazard rather than a poisoning hazard.

mcqs.stem: Which pollutants does the specification name as the causes of acid rain?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who make carbon dioxide the answer to every harmful effect of burning fuels.

options.text: Particulates and oxides of nitrogen
options.rationale: Picked by students who have one of the two causes right but swap sulfur dioxide for particulates.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons
options.rationale: Selected by students who assume every combustion pollutant shares the same harmful effects.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
options.rationale: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.

mcqs.stem: As well as causing acid rain, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen affect people directly. What effect on humans does the specification give?

options.text: They cause problems with breathing
options.rationale: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans.

options.text: They cause dimming of sunlight
options.rationale: Chosen by students who transfer the effect of particulates onto the polluting gases.

options.text: They make a hole in the ozone layer
options.rationale: Picked by students who hold one blurred idea of a damaged atmosphere in which every pollutant harms the ozone layer.

options.text: They cause skin damage from sunlight
options.rationale: Selected by students who follow the ozone idea through to sunburn, an effect the specification does not give for these gases.

mcqs.stem: Particulates in the atmosphere cause health problems for humans. What other effect does the specification give for particulates?

options.text: They add to global warming
options.rationale: Chosen by students who file every atmospheric pollutant under global warming and misread dimming as warming.

options.text: They cause global dimming
options.rationale: The specification states that particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.

options.text: They cause acid rain damage
options.rationale: Picked by students who attach acid rain to any pollutant rather than to sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

options.text: They destroy the ozone layer
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat global dimming and damage to the ozone layer as the same phenomenon.

mcqs.stem: Particulate levels in the air over a city rise year after year, and less sunlight now reaches the streets. Why do particulates have this effect?

options.text: They are suspended solids that block sunlight
options.rationale: Particulates are tiny solids suspended in the air. They reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less reaches the surface: global dimming.

options.text: They are a gas that soaks up light and heat
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat particulates as one more polluting gas rather than as solid particles suspended in the air.

options.text: They trap warmth near the Earth's surface
options.rationale: Picked by students who blur global dimming with global warming and so have particulates trapping heat instead of blocking light.

options.text: They have thinned the ozone layer above us
options.rationale: Selected by students who fold dimming, warming and ozone damage into one idea of a damaged atmosphere.

mcqs.stem: Stonework on a city building is being eaten away, and tests show the rain falling there is acidic. Which rise in air pollution explains this damage?

options.text: More sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
options.rationale: The specification gives sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen as the causes of acid rain, which is what attacks the stonework.

options.text: More carbon dioxide from the burning fuel
options.rationale: Chosen by students who make carbon dioxide the cause of acid rain because it is the pollutant they hear about most.

options.text: More carbon monoxide from car exhausts
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume every combustion pollutant shares the same harmful effects.

options.text: More particulates from sooty chimneys
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat particulates as a polluting gas like sulfur dioxide and hand them its effects.

mcqs.stem: A fuel burns with a smoky yellow flame in a limited supply of air and gives off black soot. Why is the soot produced?

options.text: The flame is so hot that it forces carbon out as solid particles
options.rationale: Chosen by students who link soot to a hot, fierce flame rather than to a shortage of air; in fact a hotter, well supplied flame burns cleanly to carbon dioxide.

options.text: The sulfur in the fuel is left behind as solid soot
options.rationale: Picked by students who think the black solid must be the sulfur impurity or ash left behind, when soot is actually unburned carbon and any sulfur leaves as sulfur dioxide gas.

options.text: The fuel breaks apart into its elements, leaving solid carbon
options.rationale: Selected by students who picture burning as splitting the fuel into its elements, rather than as some carbon failing to be oxidised because the oxygen supply is limited.

options.text: Not enough oxygen is present to oxidise all the carbon, so some is released as solid particles
options.rationale: With a limited air supply the combustion is incomplete: there is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon, so some carbon is released as fine solid particles of soot.
